title: Strain-mediated bandgap tuning and thermoelectric enhancement in monolayer group-III nitrides: a first-principles Boltzmann transport study
content: Group-III nitride monolayers (XN; X = In, Ga, Al, and B) are promising candidates for nanoelectronic, optoelectronic, and thermoelectric applications because of their tunable electronic properties, thermal stability, and favorable carrier transport characteristics. Here, density functional theory combined with semiclassical Boltzmann transport calculations is utilized to investigate the electronic and thermoelectric properties of XN monolayers under biaxial strain ranging from −7% to +7%. The effect of spin–orbit coupling (SOC) on the electronic band dispersion is also considered to assess the influence of relativistic interactions. At the relaxed state, InN, GaN, AlN, and BN show indirect bandgaps of 0.62, 2.27, 2.87, and 4.69 eV, respectively, within the PBE functional. The corresponding HSE06 bandgaps increase to 1.89, 3.69, 3.56, and 4.80 eV. Inclusion of SOC decreases the PBE bandgaps to 0.58, 1.98, 2.63, and 4.47 eV, corresponding to reductions of 6.5%, 12.8%, 8.4%, and 4.7%, respectively. The SOC effect is therefore more evident in InN and GaN than in AlN and BN. Applying biaxial strain produces substantial changes in the band structures. Indirect-to-direct bandgap transitions occur in InN, GaN, and BN at specific strain levels, whereas AlN remains indirect over the entire strain range. In addition, sufficiently large tensile strain drives InN from a semiconducting to a metallic state. The changes in the electronic bands are also reflected in the thermoelectric properties. At 300 K, InN reaches a Seebeck coefficient of 1578 µV K−1, while a maximum ZT of 1.14 is obtained under 5% compressive strain. The calculated maximum power factors are 1.70 × 1012, 81.7 × 1012, 166 × 1012, and 92.3 × 1012 W K−2 m−1 s−1 for InN, GaN, AlN, and BN, respectively. Compared with InN and GaN, AlN and BN show condition dependent variations in their thermoelectric response with applied strain, suggesting that their transport properties are less sensitive to mechanical strain. These results show that biaxial strain can be used to control both the electronic structure and thermoelectric response of XN monolayers, making them relevant for strain-tunable nanoelectronic and thermoelectric applications.
